title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures
summary: Defines the procedures for specifying and registering media types, such as those used in HTTP and MIME, with IANA. It sets out the registration trees, the rules for naming types, and how new types are reviewed. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Rules for giving every kind of file a proper name tag, such as picture or text, and for signing up new tags in a shared list.

subtitle: The rules for naming and registering media types such as text/plain with IANA, and how each registration tree is reviewed.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as HTTP and MIME can carry arbitrary labeled content, so the labels, called media types, need an orderly, well-specified and public registry.
tldr.mechanism: It defines registration trees (standards, vendor, personal and unregistered), naming and content requirements, a review and approval procedure run mostly by IANA with a Media Types Reviewer, and a registry for structured syntax suffixes such as +json.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 13), obsoletes RFC 4288 and is updated by RFC 9694.

today: RFC 6838 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 4288. It is listed as updated by RFC 9694 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and History
sections.content:
Many protocols, including HTTP and MIME, can carry arbitrary labeled content. The label is a media type: a top-level type and a subtype, which is further structured into trees, and optionally companion data called parameters. A registration process keeps these labels defined in an orderly, well-specified and public way, in the IANA central registry.

The process began for the asynchronous mail environment, where limiting the number of types helped interoperability. As media types spread to environments where many types are no hindrance, that was too restrictive. RFC 2048 loosened it, and this document now stands apart from the MIME document set to show it is independent of MIME. It obsoletes RFC 4288.
sections.eli5: Files need name tags so programs know whether they are looking at a picture or a story. A shared list stops two people from using the same tag for different things.

sections.title: Registration Trees
sections.content:
Different trees fit different needs and are told apart by a facet prefix in the subtype name.

  • Standards tree: no facet. For types of general interest. Either approved by the IESG and published as an RFC, or registered by a recognized standards-related organization under Specification Required (which implies Expert Review). The owner is the standards organization.
  • Vendor tree: facet vnd.. For types tied to publicly available products. Anyone may register, though the vendor can assert ownership. Submitted directly to IANA for Expert Review.
  • Personal or vanity tree: facet prs.. For experimental types or products not distributed commercially. Also reviewed by an expert at IANA.
  • Unregistered x. tree: facet x.. For private, local use. These cannot be registered and use is strongly discouraged. Names starting with x- are no longer part of this tree.

New top-level registration trees can be created only by IETF Standards Action.
sections.eli5: There are different shelves for the name tags: one for official standards, one for company products, one for personal projects, and a private drawer nobody checks.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.content:
A media type MUST function as an actual media format. A transfer encoding such as base64, a charset, or a collection of separate entities cannot be registered. Type and subtype names are case-insensitive and follow an ABNF that allows names of up to 127 characters, but SHOULD be limited to 64 characters. The characters before the first dot give the facet, and the characters after the last plus give a structured syntax suffix.

Each top-level type has its own rules. For text, a charset parameter SHOULD be required, UTF-8 SHOULD be the default if one is chosen, and relying on the US-ASCII default is no longer permitted. application is for data that does not fit elsewhere, multipart and message follow RFC 2046, and a new top-level type needs a Standards Track RFC.

Every registered type MUST have a single canonical data format. Standards-tree types MUST have a permanent, readily available public specification. Vendor and personal types may keep format details private, though a public specification is encouraged. Parameters MUST be fully specified in the standards tree, and new parameters SHOULD NOT be defined as a way to add functionality there. Types using a registered structured syntax SHOULD use its +suffix, and MUST NOT use a suffix for a syntax they do not employ.
sections.eli5: A name tag must describe a real kind of file, follow the spelling rules, and say how the file is built so others can read it.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registration is described as an administrative procedure, not a formal standards process, meant to allow community comment and sanity checking without excessive delay. IETF registrations in the standards tree follow normal IETF processes, starting with an Internet-Draft.

Notice of a standards-tree registration SHOULD go to the media-types@iana.org list for review. For other trees this is optional but encouraged. Standards-tree requests from other organizations, and vendor and personal requests, go directly to IANA, which passes them to the Media Types Reviewer appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director(s). Substandard requests are returned. Reviewer decisions can be appealed to the IESG. A new standards organization needs IESG recognition first.

A provisional registration lets standards-tree names be assigned early, with only the name and contact information required. It lives in a separate public list and may be updated or abandoned at any time.

Registrations cannot be deleted. An unwanted type can be marked OBSOLETE. The owner may request changes using the same procedure as the original registration, and the IESG can reassign ownership when the author is out of contact.
sections.eli5: You fill in a form, people can comment, a reviewer checks it, and then it goes on the list. Entries can be retired but never erased.

sections.title: The Registration Template and Suffix Registry
sections.content:
The registration template has fields for type and subtype name, required and optional parameters, encoding considerations, security considerations, interoperability considerations, published specification, applications that use the type, fragment identifier considerations, additional information, contact, intended usage, restrictions on usage, author and change controller.

Encoding considerations take one of four values: 7bit, 8bit, binary or framed. Intended usage is one of COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE. Optional additional information includes magic numbers, file extensions and Macintosh file type codes.

The document also sets up a separate structured syntax suffix registry for suffixes such as +der, +fastinfoset and +json. A suffix request carries its own template (name, suffix, references, encoding, interoperability, fragment and security considerations, contact and change controller) and goes through Expert Review. Its initial contents are in RFC 6839.
sections.eli5: The form asks the same questions for every type, such as what it is called, how it is built and what could go wrong.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
A security analysis MUST be done for every standards-tree type, and is encouraged but not required for vendor and personal types. Descriptions must be as accurate as possible. A registration MUST NOT say there are "no security issues associated with this type"; vendor and personal types MAY say the issues have not been assessed. Suffix registrations cannot use that option.

Issues to examine include active content, directives that disclose information, compression that expands enormously, and types that rely on external security services. Types SHOULD state whether they use compression, and MUST say whether they employ active content.
sections.eli5: Every new file type must say honestly what dangers it could bring, and it may not just claim it is perfectly safe.
